name: Maya Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on fryers and prep at The Anchor, a pub restaurant on Mill Road. I get in at ten, peel and chip about forty kilos of potatoes, batter the fish, then it's the lunch rush and I don't look up till three. Gary, the head chef, still checks every plate I send because I'm slow on the garnish. I like the noise when it's packed, honestly, but my wrists ache by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The split shifts wear me out, ten till three then back at five till close, for lower pay than the cooks at the hotel get. What keeps me there is the crew, and the fact there's nowhere else in town, just the hotel and a chain pizza place. Dev, my partner, packs boxes at the warehouse, so between us we cover rent and not much else. I've got about two hundred in the bank, which is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I've heard enough about robots taking our jobs. At work we'd probably laugh about it, Gary would say he told us so. I don't post much online, but I'd share something saying the bosses should stop using AI as an excuse to keep wages down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't fix anything for me. The Anchor still cuts my hours every January when it goes quiet, and the rent on our flat went up again in March. My problem was never robots, it's that kitchen pay is rubbish and there's two hundred in my account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and try to pick up extra Sundays when the carvery's on. I'd cut the takeaways Dev and I get on Friday, that's about thirty a week. And I'd ask Gary again about a pay rise once I've done a full year on the fryers without a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a day, then back to normal worry. Normal worry is checking the bank app before I buy a coffee. It's tiring, but I'm used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said January is when hours get cut. What happens in your house that month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last January I went down to three shifts a week for six weeks. We paid rent late once and the landlord sent a letter, which scared me more than anything about AI. Dev did overtime at the warehouse and we lived on pasta and toast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone at work talked about a union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who does the bar, keeps a hospitality union leaflet on the staff noticeboard. I haven't joined yet because it's about ten a month and I keep telling myself next month. If nothing changes with AI, the low pay is still the thing a union should fight about.

say: I'd say **good riddance** to the robot hype and get back to talking about pay.
I'd post that bosses shouldn't use AI as an **excuse for low wages**.
think: My real problem is **low kitchen pay** and two hundred in the bank, not robots.
The Anchor still cuts my **January hours**, so the hard months stay hard.
do: Pick up **extra Sunday shifts** on the carvery to cover the quiet months.
Cut the Friday takeaways and save about **thirty a week**.
Ask the head chef for a **pay rise** after a full year on fryers.
feel: **Relief** that lasts a day, then the usual **money worry** comes back.
S0.quote: We paid rent late once and the landlord sent a letter, which scared me more than anything about AI.
fieldNote: Maya's **winter hour cuts** and a late rent letter shape her more than any technology story.
She frames everything through **pay and bosses**, even when AI fades away.
She has thought about the union for months but keeps **putting off** the ten-a-month fee.

steps.text: Work extra Sunday carvery shifts at The Anchor through the winter
Stop the Friday takeaway with Dev to save thirty a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem first, not ours, because no computer is battering cod. But I'd also say watch what the owners do with the money they save. Online I'd share stuff about protecting workers, that's my side of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it creeps into the kitchen through the back door. The ordering, the rota, the stock counts, those go to software, and then Gary has more time to watch how slow I am. And if the warehouse puts in more robots, my partner's job goes before mine, and then we can't make rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally join the union, this time for real, in the first month. I'd put twenty a week into a separate account so there's something if Dev loses shifts. I wouldn't touch any of the AI apps, I just don't trust them and my phone's too old anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a slow leak. Nothing dramatic, but I'd be watching the warehouse news every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dev's job might go first. What would you two do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would probably try the supermarket or driving, and I'd ask for every shift going. We've talked about moving in with his mum in the next town if it got bad, but she's got a one-bed flat. I'd hate that, sleeping on a sofa bed at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, the kitchen porter, who's fifty-eight and does the washing up and the bins. If they get one of those dish robots, he's done, and he's got nowhere to go. He's the one who taught me to sharpen a knife properly.

say: I'd say this hits **office jobs first**, because no computer is battering cod.
I'd tell people to watch where the **owners' savings** go, not the shiny tools.
think: The **ordering and rota** going to software gives the head chef more time to watch me.
If the warehouse automates, **Dev's job** goes first and we can't cover rent.
do: Join the **hospitality union** in the first month for about ten a month.
Put **twenty a week** into a separate account in case Dev loses shifts.
Stay away from **AI apps**, because I don't trust them and my phone's too old.
feel: A **slow leak** of worry that never quite stops.
S1.quote: If the warehouse puts in more robots, my partner's job goes before mine, and then we can't make rent.
fieldNote: Maya sees the danger through her **partner's warehouse job**, not her own fryer.
She would finally act on the **union**, which she treats as her one real lever.
Her refusal of AI tools is partly distrust and partly an **old phone**.

steps.text: Join the hospitality union Priya keeps pinned on the staff noticeboard
Move twenty a week into a separate rainy-day account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let this happen with no plan for people like us. At work I'd be the one going on about how the government should tax the companies making the robots. Online I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the cooking part buys me about three years, until the robots come in 2031. But the warehouse is mostly screens and scanners and conveyors, so Dev's in trouble almost straight away. I can't think of anything I'm qualified for that a robot can't do by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard on the union, go to meetings, push for a deal on notice and retraining at The Anchor. I'd cancel the gym and the phone upgrade and save whatever we can, maybe forty a week. If Dev loses his job, we'd have to ask about housing help, which I'd do even though I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. Two years is nothing. I'm still learning to fry and they're talking about the end of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we don't panic, we make a list. Then I'd probably cry in the bathroom so he doesn't see. He gets quiet when he's worried and I get loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, which is twenty-five a month, and the streaming. Then the car insurance if Dev's job goes, because we'd sell the car. Food we don't really cut, because we already eat cheap.

say: I'd say letting AGI arrive with **no plan** for workers is madness.
I'd push for **taxing robot companies** and sign every petition going.
think: Cooking buys me roughly **three years**, until the robots arrive around 2031.
**Dev's warehouse job** goes almost straight away, because it's screens and conveyors.
I can't name anything I'm **qualified for** that robots can't do by then.
do: Go to **union meetings** and push The Anchor for a deal on notice and retraining.
Cancel the gym and phone upgrade to save **forty a week**.
Ask about **housing help** if Dev loses his job.
feel: **Properly scared**, because two years feels like nothing.
**Unfinished**, still learning to fry while the job's end is announced.
S2.quote: I'm still learning to fry and they're talking about the end of the job.
fieldNote: Maya expects the household to lose **Dev's income** within months of AGI.
She turns fear into **collective action** and petitions rather than personal plans.
She would accept **public help**, which fits her views but still costs her pride.

steps.text: Attend union meetings and push for a notice and retraining deal
Cancel the gym and the phone upgrade to save forty a week
Apply for housing help if Dev's warehouse job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, I'd say workers need a say before this lands. I'd talk about it in the staff room, maybe get people to come to a union meeting. I'd vote for whoever promises a proper safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a bit better, because I'd have about eight before robots fry fish as well as me. But I'm not good at learning new things, I never was at school. So I'd probably just be the same cook, eight years older, with nothing behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save, properly, fifty a week if Dev keeps his hours, so there's a few thousand by the time it comes. I'd get the union to push for training money from the government, not from my own pocket. And I'd vote, which I didn't do last time, I'm ashamed to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less like a cliff and more like walking downhill in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at learning new things. Is there anything you would try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe care work, like my aunt does in the care home. Robots can't hold someone's hand, I don't think. But I'd want the care course paid for, because I can't afford to drop shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the head chef what you're planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not Gary. He's alright, but he'd think I'm halfway out the door and give my Sundays to someone else. I'd keep my head down until I had something sorted.

say: I'd say **workers need a say** before AGI lands in kitchens.
I'd vote for whoever promises a proper **safety net**.
think: Five years gives me roughly **eight before robots** fry fish as well as me.
I'm **slow at learning** new things, so I'd likely stay the same cook with nothing behind me.
do: Save **fifty a week** while Dev's hours hold, aiming for a few thousand.
Push the union for **government training money**, not my own.
**Vote** in the next election, unlike last time.
feel: **Heavy**, like walking downhill in the dark.
S3.quote: Robots can't hold someone's hand, I don't think. But I'd want the care course paid for, because I can't afford to drop shifts.
fieldNote: The extra years ease the panic but Maya still expects to **lose the job**.
She doubts her own **ability to learn**, a feeling carried from school.
**Care work** is her only imagined exit, and only if someone else pays.

steps.text: Save fifty a week while Dev's warehouse hours hold
Push the union to win government-paid training for cooks
Register and vote for the party promising a safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it fairly, so no excuses. I'd tell people at work we should plan together, not each on our own. Online I'd share stuff about free courses for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, plus three for robots, means I'm forty when the fryer robot turns up. That actually scares me more in a weird way, because forty is late to start again. But it's also enough time to get a proper qualification if someone helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the care certificate at the college in the evenings, the one my aunt did, within the first year if it's free. I'd keep my shifts at The Anchor the whole time. I'd stay in the union and keep pushing for paid study time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but a bit more in charge of it. Like there's a road, even if I'm bad at roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually sign up for the course rather than putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my aunt came with me to the open day, honestly. And if it was Monday nights, my one free evening. I put things off when I'm scared of looking stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would money look in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight, same as now, unless the union wins better pay. I'd try to keep a month's rent saved, which would be a first for me. Dev wants a dog, but that waits.

say: I'd say ten years means **no excuses** for doing this unfairly.
I'd tell the crew we should **plan together**, not each on our own.
think: I'd be **forty** when the fryer robot turns up, late to start again.
Ten years is enough for a **proper qualification** if someone helps me.
do: Start the **care certificate** at college on Monday evenings within a year.
Keep **every shift** at The Anchor while I study.
Stay in the union and push for **paid study time**.
feel: **Worried**, but a bit more **in charge** of it.
S4.quote: Ten years, plus three for robots, means I'm forty when the fryer robot turns up.
fieldNote: Maya does the **date maths** herself and fixes on being forty.
Her blocker is **fear of looking stupid**, not lack of interest.
She would only start the course with her **aunt's company** and a free evening.

steps.text: Start the evening care certificate at the local college on Mondays
Keep all shifts at The Anchor while studying
Push through the union for paid study time for kitchen staff

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because Dev and I would both be out within a few years and we've got nothing saved. What would help is the government making the robot companies pay into a fund for people like us, and free training I can do around my shifts. A union deal at The Anchor would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about rent. Everyone talks about jobs, but if rent keeps climbing like it has, I'm in trouble in every one of your five pictures. Fix housing and I could face the rest.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but if rent keeps climbing like it has, I'm in trouble in every one of your five pictures.
portrait: Maya is a 27-year-old **fryer and prep cook** at a busy pub restaurant, still learning and paid less than most.
She lives with Dev, a **warehouse packer**, with about two hundred in the bank.
She sees every scenario through **pay, rent and bosses**, and trusts unions more than technology.
She is **anxious** even in AI Plateau and alarmed by fast AGI, mostly for Dev's job.
Her one escape idea is **care work**, but only with free training and her aunt's help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Dev would both lose work with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **robot company fund** and free training she can fit around shifts.
A **union deal** at The Anchor and lower rent.
